utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence -- oh, I'm sorry, the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; legal intern, Sarah Munsch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Philipp Mueller, legal intern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe so. We're having some technical problems with my Case Manager, but I think for the time being, we'll be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 2434, which is tab 836.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you recognise the two men that we're seeing in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the uniform is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan; and the person in the white shirt is Boro Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is the same Boro Zivanovic that we were talking about yesterday as the person who was the president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3218. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please move into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, yesterday we looked at the Law on Territorial Organisation, Article 14, and we saw there and talked a bit about the -- the fact that the government of the SBWS had authority to choose those persons who would serve as Executive Council members for the municipalities. Do you remember that? Those people were chosen by the government.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but those people were not elected by the government, just confirmed by the government. The government elected presidents of the Executive Councils who formed their own teams by themselves, and they would then propose a list to the government which would generally be accepted. We didn't have to know all of these people and theoretically it wasn't possible to know all of these people because it was a matter for the president of the Executive Council who had been given the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, under your own legislation, the Executive Councils' responsibility was to implement and answer to -- I should say implement SBWS government policy and to answer to the SBWS government. We agree on that? That's how it was envisaged in the legislation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it said in the law and in some theoretical way you could not be responsible to the government that was not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the last word Mr. Hadzic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the last word of your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not have been responsible to some other government of some other state who was not from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so when we see Mr. Zivanovic here doing the things that we've been talking about this morning and at the end of yesterday, what we're seeing is that this is a person who is shown himself willing to implement SBWS government policy in his municipality of Beli Manastir; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic was elected as the president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council at a time when the government had not yet been formed, and since the territory of Beli Manastir municipality was almost 100% preserved during war operations, they had a completely preserved cadre structure, so he was elected to this position by the citizens of Beli Manastir. The government confirmed what the citizens of Beli Manastir elected only at the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, the interpreters are asking if you can please try to slow down in your answers.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Not to drag this out too long, but we looked at it yesterday, the decision appointing Mr. Zivanovic to be the president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council is a decision that appears over your name, over your approval; correct? And we understand the process that led to that, but in order to make that happen, it has to be approved and signed off on by you, and that's what you did. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to you, I am not a lawyer so I am surprised by the way you put your question. This was adopted by the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and I signed the decision of the government. I was the president of the government, equal -- the first among equals, and this was the proposal of the citizens of Beli Manastir. The government accepted that, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 562, Exhibit P2400.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, the last document that we looked at was dated 1st of September, 1992. Now this is an article from "The Independent," from the 27th of September, 1992. So a few weeks later. And in the text here, as you can see at the very beginning, Mr. Zivanovic is quoted as saying: "This is now the land of the Serbian people. And so it will stay for the next thousand years. If the Croats do not like it, we will start a new war." Moving down to the fourth paragraph, it says that: "More than 50 Hungarians and Croats have been murdered in recent weeks. No suspects have been arrested. Almost every Croatian church in the region has been blown up. No Catholic priests are tolerated. In this UN-protected zone, Croats and Hungarians have no protection against Serbs, who rob them, beat them, expel them from their homes or kill them. At the same time, the local authorities are bussing in Bosnian Serb refugees to fill vacated Croatian or Hungarian homes. Once inside, the Serbs are not allowed out again." Mr. Hadzic, you were fully aware of this campaign of terror and persecution that was being directed against non-Serbs in Beli Manastir during this period of time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I don't see a link between this newspaper article and myself or your question about this article, for that matter. These things in the article are so nebulous that they are really impossible to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if you're someone who got a family member killed or if you're someone who was driven out because you weren't Serb probably wouldn't be so nebulous to you. We're not talking about nebulous things; we're talk about a campaign of violence and terror. And I'm asking you, sir, you knew about this. You had to have known about this. It was simply too big for you not to know about.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, when I said "nebulous things," I did not have the victims in mind. I empathiee with the victims. Both my family and myself suffered. I'm talking about refugees being bussed in from Bosnia. Those things are nebulous. In 1991, they were propaganda. And even those with little information know that this is not true. And we are discussing things now as if it were 1991 and not 2014. What refugees would have arrived from Bosnia in 1991 when Bosnia was still not in war? I apologise for using the term "nebulous" but I don't know what else to use. Refugees, in Beli Manastir, from Bosnia, in 1991, and especially I can't comment upon other people's words, quoting Borivoje Zivanovic. I was not present when he said that. He never told me anything about that. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me put my question to you again because you did not answer it. This campaign of terror and violence directed against non-Serbs in Beli Manastir is something that you knew about. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I didn't know. The conflicted lasted for a relatively short time in Beli Manastir. After that, military authorities took hold. And whatever I heard about any unlawful acts, people were arrested and prosecuted, to the best of the ability of the government in which I was the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think you're mistaken. In your previous answer a moment ago you seemed to think that this is from 1991, questioning why would Serb refugees be coming from Bosnia in 1991, I think I mentioned at the beginning -- this is September 1992; September 27th of 1992. So in fact the conflict was fully engaged in Bosnia at that time, and there would have been refugees from all three groups fleeing Bosnia. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information to that effect. I don't know that refugees came to Baranja from Bosnia at any time. Whatever I heard, I can only tell you that refugees were from Western Slavonia and from some cities in Croatia. This is the first time I hear that somebody thought that they were coming from Bosnia. Those refugees had to arrive from and through Bosnia because they did not have a territorial contact with Baranja via any other territory or via any other state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if representatives of international organisations, such as UNPROFOR and other international organisations, are present in Beli Manastir writing about a campaign -- what is essentially a campaign of violence and terror against non-Serbs and if articles are being published about it in the press, here the foreign press, this is all information that you in fact didn't know yourself?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew and what I could deal with resulted in trials. You mentioned UNPROFOR here as if UNPROFOR had been there as tourists and is -- as if they were international monitors in white clothes. They accepted the responsibility to provide security for all of the population in the whole territory when they took over the responsibility for the territory from the JNA. It applied across the board. They were not tourist there. They were not rapporteurs or reporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. So your government, your people aren't responsible for protecting all of the population in the area that you control? Now you're passing that responsibility off to UNPROFOR. You're washing your hands of this. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we know in the context of the question what does it mean "your government"? Is it the government of the SBWS or RSK government and on which period it is related to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you clarify, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is September 1992. This is the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel's right. It is not your government. Rather, it is a body, an Executive Council, that exists within your republic. That is, the republic that you're a president of. Rather than blaming UNPROFOR and others for doing the work that your government -- sorry, the RSK government should have been doing, perhaps the RSK government and its president should have been doing more on its own to protect non-Serbs, such as removing someone like Borivoje Zivanovic from his position; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of your question, you said that I shifted blame and washed my hands off. I'm not saying that UNPROFOR was to blame. I'm saying that the Serbian people who tried to implement laws in the territory and UNPROFOR had a joint task and split the responsibility of providing normal life for everybody in the area. As far as my engagement is concerned, I did my best to carry out my part of the task. It was a well-known fact how authorities functioned and in whose competence that was, generally speaking. But it was not just the obligation of the Serbian side, an unilateral obligation; UNPROFOR had the same obligation. If not an equal share of -- of -- of the obligation or more of the obligation, then at least an equal share. I'm not saying that I'm washing my hands of all responsibility and that I'm shifting blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if we could go to page 2 of this in the English. And it's the second full paragraph under the heading that says page 76. So it would also be page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You mention UNPROFOR, Mr. Hadzic. There's a reference in this paragraph to a statement by Blandine Negga, an UN civil affairs co-ordinator in eastern Croatia. You heard her evidence in this trial. The fact is she was constantly trying to bring to your attention and the attention to other Serb authorities in the area the level of crime and violence directed at non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this question and to this assertion, I first have to say that technically this is not correct. Ms. Negga, whom I respect a lot, said it herself here, that she could never communicate with me directly, and you say, "she sent this to you." When you say "to you," who do you mean? Do you mean me personally? The question sounded to me as if Ms. Negga sent this to me, and that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that she was constantly attempting to bring these issues to the attention of your subordinate, that is, others who were members of -- Serbian authorities in the region?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Define what you mean when you say "my subordinates." And based on what law would they have been subordinated to me? Apart from my secretary or my driver, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to this, Mr. Hadzic, when we talk about your powers as president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 3 of this document, fourth paragraph from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your direct examination, Mr. Hadzic, and I came back to it already in the cross, we discussed the incident involving Arkan and members of the UNPROFOR battalion, the Belgian battalion at the Batina bridge. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the fourth full paragraph from the bottom of this, it appears that Mr. Zivanovic, Borivoje Zivanovic, does not have good relations with the peacekeepers either. He says: "They are worse than the Ustasha Croatian Fascists active during the Second World War. Only the swastika is missing." You were in fact aware, Mr. Hadzic, of Mr. Zivanovic's dissatisfaction with the UNPROFOR peacekeepers in Beli Manastir. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic never said that to me, not in so many words. Actually, we never discussed that topic. He was the president of the municipality, and he was in direct communication with the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, he was in direct communication with you as well, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were on speaking terms. When I saw him, we greeted the -- each other, but as far as this matter is concerned, we did not share the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 561, 65 ter 1278.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is an article from "Politika." 26th of September is the date of the publication, 1992. So this is just one day before "The Independent" article that we were just looking at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may I ask to zoom in the B/C/S text, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The name of the article is "Goran Hadzic in Baranja: We are in favour of peace and agreement." Do you have that article, Mr. Hadzic? Are you able to see at least the first two columns of it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the first half of the text, the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is putting you in Beli Manastir on the 25th of September, 1992. The end of the first paragraph it reports that you've said that: "If Croatia wants war, it will have it to the bitter end."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would suggest if the witness could see whole B/C/S text before he answers the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I disagree. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm listening, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, this is all new, as far as I know, in this trial. I know the Defence's preference was to put hard copies to the accused. We're following the procedure that's been followed from day one. All of these things are on the list that went across to the Defence. If they want to make the image smaller so he can see more of it. But I -- I disagree, Mr. President. And, frankly, if I may respectfully suggest that the number of interruptions seems to be increasing on matters that aren't justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we're banned to show to Mr. Hadzic the Prosecution's list because suggestions of the Prosecution. And because of that, Mr. Hadzic is entitled to see this document at least before he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He can have my copy, Mr. President. The text is small. I don't know if he can read it. With your permission, we could at least try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's not a bad idea, Mr. Stringer. You realise, of course, Mr. Stringer, that Mr. Zivanovic is right about the ban.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The ban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Defence was not allowed to show -- to show your documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do. I stand corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you able to read that, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letters are very small. However, I was able to read the first part on the screen. I can provide a comment on the Prosecutor's question. This is very clear. In the title I say, "We are in favour of peace an agreement." What follows is that we will wage a war only if Croatia wants that, because we do not want it. That would be my answer to your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I actually hadn't -- I don't know that I had actually put a question to you yet. The first question was going to be simply whether you remember being in Beli Manastir on this day, 25th of September, and making an address.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely. But I suppose that that was the case, since it was published in a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to move down three paragraphs to the paragraph that begins with the words: "Misunderstandings between official, civilian authorities, and representatives of UNPROFOR ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll just continue to read: "... were most characteristic of Baranja. According to the president of the Beli Manastir municipality, Borivoje Zivanovic, since the very arrival of the Belgian-Luxembourg battalion to this area, members of Lieutenant-Colonel Zanmari Zoken's unit permanently favoured Croats. "In Zivanovic's opinion, even in those critical days when the return of the refugees to Baranja was announced, the Belgians did not succeed in hiding their favour for the Croatian side." And it continues on, says: "We demand and we shall do it officially through ours RSK government that the UN forces of Baranja, pertaining to the Belgian-Luxembourg battalion be withdrawn from Baranja, said Zivanovic." And then continues: "Hadzic agreed with that statement and promised that the government was going to officially forward the request to the competent authorities." Now, Mr. Hadzic, this raises a few questions. First of all, again, I'm going to put it to you that your presence there in Beli Manastir on the 25th of September is such that you would have been fully aware of the campaign of violence and terror directed against non-Serbs that we've been seeing about -- that we've been seeing in the earlier documents from this very same period of time. You did know about it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you basing your inference from? I couldn't find anything in the text. I did know some things and I'm willing to share my knowledge with you. But in the text, I am not able to find any references to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting there are. I'm suggesting to you that as president of the RSK who was there on the ground with Mr. Zivanovic, you were aware of what was going on in this area of Beli Manastir. Your presence there and your position put you into knowledge of what was happening there. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't have to mean that. My presence there was for the opposite reason, to deal with the problems that were present all over the territory of the RSK, to prevent them, and to process those who were involved in committing crimes against anybody, Serbs and Croats, and the like. We had similar problems not only in Baranja but all over the place. We had problems with UNPROFOR everywhere. The Belgian battalion was nothing special. We had similar problems and objections against the French battalion. A couple of months before this meeting, in June, there was the Croatian operation on the Miljevac plateau and UNPROFOR did not protect the population, and we had objections. In the previous text, someone imputed to Borivoje Zivanovic that he mentioned swastika in some of his speeches. This is not true. He didn't say that. And obviously there were objections against the work of UNPROFOR, the Belgians, the French, the Russians, and everybody else. I promise that in my contacts with the representatives of UNPROFOR I was trying to deal with those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then if that's the case, Mr. Hadzic, then what you've told us a few minutes ago is not true, because a few minutes ago before we showed you this document, I asked you, I said: "You were in fact aware, Mr. Hadzic, of Mr. Zivanovic's dissatisfaction with the UNPROFOR peacekeepers in Beli Manastir. True?" And you said that: "Mr. Zivanovic never said that to me, not in so many words." I'm looking at page 18, line 1: "Actually, we never discussed that topic. He was the president of the municipality, and he was in direct communication with the government."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just confirmed my words. I never heard Zivanovic mention Fascist or a swastika. I've never heard those before. I told you that Mr. Zivanovic was an official of the government -- or, rather, he reported back to the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. These are two separate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you did not tell the truth when I asked you a few minutes ago whether you had discussed with Mr. Zivanovic, whether you were aware of his dissatisfaction with UNPROFOR. In fact now you're telling us you were. And you've only admitted it because I showed it to you in the document.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. You misunderstood me completely. You mentioned Fascists, a swastika, and I said that I never heard it before. At that meeting I did not talk to Mr. Zivanovic. There were at least 15 or 20 other people at that meeting. Everybody was engaged in conversations, including Mr. Zivanovic. Dissatisfaction with UNPROFOR existed not only in Baranja, but also in Slavonia, in the Knin area, in Dalmatia, everywhere. It was a notorious fact that there was a lot of dissatisfaction with the work of UNPROFOR everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were aware of Mr. Zivanovic's dissatisfaction; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I see that he mentioned that at the press conference. Maybe somebody else from Baranja told me that and not Zivanovic, about the Belgian battalion and minor problems, but I never thought that it would be the same level with Fascism. I've heard it only today from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You just said, "Maybe somebody else from Baranja told me that ..." This article puts you in Beli Manastir with Zivanovic, and here you support him and you agree with his statement and you say that the government is going to officially forward the request to the competent authorities to have the Belgian battalion removed. I mean, you are completely with Mr. Zivanovic on this issue of UNPROFOR, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this was the journalist's comment. I said that I would pass it on to the government as far as my authority went to sent a protest because of the Belgian battalion's conduct. But I did not want the Belgian battalion to withdraw, nor was that under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 411, which is L57.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as that's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, I can tell you what we're going to do now is talk a little bit about the Executive Council for Vukovar municipality. It would be page 98 of the English. This, again, is from the Gazette. And in the B/C/S, the page is going to be ending with the numbers 9351 in the upper right-hand corner. So about 23 pages down. I'm looking at the law -- the decision to appoint the Executive Council of Vukovar Municipality. Do you have that, Mr. Hadzic? At least --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is the -- referring to a session held on the 4th of December, 1991 and here we see five individuals appointed to the Executive Council of Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if we could just go to the end of the decision, the bottom, just so that we can see the date and the approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this would appear to have been approved by you on the 5th of December, 1991, as prime minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this a couple of minutes ago. This was adopted by the government, and I signed it as a government decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we know and -- well, you're -- the adoption by the government and you're signing it as the prime minister in fact is the procedure that's envisioned under your own legislation. You're just exercising the authority that exists under your own legislation. Nothing unusual or remarkable about this, is there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's how I understand it. I'm not sure I understand it in the best way. But I was supposed to sign each government decision, and if I was not there, if I was absent, then it should have been signed by the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, and these people were appointed to the Executive Council because, again, they could be counted on to implement and carry out SBWS policy. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the theoretical sense, the way you're putting it, that would seem like that. However, it was not actually like that. We had problems in setting up the civilian authorities in the municipality of Vukovar. We found one person who satisfied both the fighters from the city and from the villages, because he was from Negoslavci but was working in Vukovar. So that this was a compromise that was approved. And later Srbobran Bibic formed his team by himself and proposed that the government just give its formal approval. We didn't know most of these people. I didn't know them, and the ministers in particular didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You just said that, "We found one person who satisfied the fighters." And would that be number one here, Mr. Vujovic, Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know Miroljub Vujovic was a fighter at the time. Well, there was this combat. The fighters' group, they were against the government. They felt the government sat in Erdut, didn't do anything. They wanted to form a parallel government as a fighters' government and then I tried to find a solution there that would make everybody happy, and that is why Srbobran Bibic was proposed. But then he a problem in resolving that particular problem in the field so he, in turn, put somebody's name forward. It was no longer up to the government. It was Srbobran Bibic's discretionary right to form his own team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic was the Petrova Gora TO commander on the day that Vukovar fell; correct? If I can just -- before you begin, just to save us time, I know it's your position that you're going to say that you didn't know that at that time. You're going to say that you didn't know Vujovic was the TO commander on the 18th of November. And I know that's your position. But can we agree now, at least based on what you may have learned later, that he was in fact the TO commander, Petrova Gora, on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is correct, that I found out about it later and that later was when I came here, to the Detention Unit and when I heard that from people who were with me at the time. At the time when they were in Vukovar, I don't have to name the person who told me that, that it was at Sljivancanin's proposal. The JNA appointed him as the TO commander within two days, TO Vukovar. And then they were the ones who were supposed to sign that, but upon the insistence that he be appointed he was actually appointed on the 18th as you said. This is something that I heard here. Even three years ago I didn't know that at the time he was the commander of the Vukovar TO. I thought it was Dusan Jaksic who was at that position. I had met Jaksic at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're also aware that Miroljub Vujovic was convicted of his involvement in the 200 or so executions that occurred at Ovcara - correct? - on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, just like you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it turns out that he managed to get himself appointed to the Vukovar Executive Council on the 5th of December, 1991. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he managed to get himself elected or if his name was put forward by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1495, 65 ter 6080.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 21st of January, 1992. And this is the Secretariat of National Defence of Vukovar. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And before I ask you about that, it appears here that Mr. Vujovic now is the secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence. Could you please tell us what was the Secretariat of National Defence and what was Mr. Vujovic's position, or what did that -- that position involve?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that now precisely because this is not my profession or field of interest, but I know that this was appointed by the president of the municipality. It was a secretariat that dealt with mobilisation and that sort of thing, those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were aware that Mr. Vujovic held this position in January of 1992? Again, I understand your position. You didn't know about his background as TO commander and involvement at Ovcara, but setting that aside, do you agree that he was in this position as of 21 January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that he was, but I most sincerely would like to say that I do not recall that I knew that at the time or that anybody was obliged to tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what you're seeing here, in any event, is not something that you have -- you don't doubt that or question that at this point?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to question it or to confirm it in any particular way, because I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3219. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 532, Exhibit P1879.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is now moving out to August of 1992 in Vukovar. This is coming from the RSK MUP. And it's reporting on a number of things. The one I wanted to ask you about is at the bottom of page 1 of the English. It's the fourth paragraph of the document. The paragraph begins with the words: "With the previous oral approval of the president ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "... of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Goran Hadzic, on 31 July, 1992, a Crisis Staff was formed in Vukovar comprising Vukovar Executive Council President ... Visic; Deputy Executive Council President, Mirko Jagetic; the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, Miroljub Vujovic; Vukovar SUP chief, Dragan Djukic; and the commander of the TO Staff, Zoran Vranjesevic. According to the conclusions of the first meeting of the Crisis Staff ...," according to this document, it continues: "... they intend to suspend all RSK laws and introduce people's tribunals that would pass on-the-spot sentences ranging from acquittal to execution. Police chief Milos Vojnovic and Vukovar court president who attended the meeting opposed these conclusions." Mr. Hadzic, do you recall giving an oral approval as president on the 31st of July or giving an oral approval that authorised the formation of this Crisis Staff that's referred to here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I don't think I gave that or ever discussed that with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, did you become aware that, as is indicated here, there were some people who were actually opposing what sounds to be sort of a vigilante law, this people's tribunal. Did you hear talk of trying to establish people's tribunals in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm hearing this here for the first time. I didn't even read that in these papers that I received. Perhaps it just skipped my attention among the papers that I received. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When did you learn that Miroljub Vujovic had actually been the TO commander, Petrova Gora, as of the time that Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask redaction of this last answer of Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think our position would be that, so far, counsel has failed to say why a redaction would be justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was more or less waiting for that, Mr. Zivanovic. Should we go into private session to discuss this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you are aware that shortly after the fall of Vukovar and the events, the crime that occurred at Ovcara on the 20th of November, Miroljub Vujovic was among those fighters who actually went back to Belgrade and was received by the JNA leadership as part of a ceremony and a dinner. It was widely reported. You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at the time. I saw that here in some footage, and I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could have tab 972, P2287. And we'll wait to hear from the interpreters. This is a video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "On the occasion of the completion of combat activities, Army General Veljko Kadijevic and his -- on the occasion of completion of combat activities in the area of Vukovar, Army General Veljko Kadijevic received at the Federal Secretariat for National Defence several of his commander who participated in military operations in this area. "Reporter: Army General Veljko Kadijevic and his associates made a reception on the occasion of completion of combat activities in the area of Vukovar for the following personnel: Commander of the 1st Military District, Lieutenant-General Zivota Panic; commander of the Operative Group 'North,' Major-General Andrija Biorcevic; commander of Operative Defence 'South,' Colonel Mile Mrksic; and commander of airborne unit of the First Air Force and Anti-aircraft Defence Corps, Colonel Branislav Petkovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've stopped it there, Mr. Hadzic. The name was mentioned. Did you recognise General Biorcevic there in the line?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot see it on this footage anymore but I did see him at the beginning of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if and when you see Mr. Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll continue now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "He complemented them for their triumph. The Federal Secretariat for National Defence stated that the reception was also attended by several commanding officers, soldiers, and volunteers who distinguished themselves during the fierce fighting in the streets and catacombs of the fortified city. In a lengthy conversation, General Kadijevic commented all the participants of an almost two-month long battle which ended in a bitter defeat and in capturing of the elite Ustasha formations and of numerous ZNG /National Guard Corps/ and foreign mercenaries. Pointing out that the success in a combat endeavour, fearlessness and striving of the commanding officers, soldiers, and volunteers demonstrated in the Vukovar operation, shall represent a great boost and an inspiration to all soldiers and commanding officers in the Yugoslav People's Army."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. There is Vujovic, the third person from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hadzic we just learned that you have identified him. You said he is the third person from the end. Can you describe what he is wearing.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A new green uniform that he had received that morning so that he could change into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How do you know that he received the uniform that morning?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without moving into private session, this is something that I had heard here once I arrived. And then it will be clear to you how I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think we need to do that, Mr. President, unless it's the Chamber's wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you want to add something, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I recognised General Aco Vasiljevic here also. He was at the meeting. It's the person who testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And which one is he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him there, at the table. They were wearing ceremonial uniform, not combat uniforms, but ceremonial uniforms. He was sitting at the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have -- Mr. President, actually -- actually, I could probably do this document in two minutes. Tab 1502, P00329.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Staying with this issue of Executive Councils, Mr. Hadzic, I wanted to take a look at what was happening in Bapska at that level. This is the 13th of February, 1992. Minutes of a meeting held 12th February, 1992, in Bapska between local civilian authorities and the assistant commander for civilian affairs. And this then goes on to describe what was discussed at the meeting. There's a reference to a Mr. Savicin, secretary, Mr. Kulic, and five members of the Executive Council. Also members of the local commune are there, as well as the TO commander and his deputy and others whose names we can see. Someone from the Bapska staff TO. TO Staff named Janic and another one named Jaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my screen doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shall we take a break, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the time anyway, Mr. President. Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Stringer. There's a sort oral ruling I would like to read out. On 23 June, 2014, the Defence filed a motion in which it seeks an order pursuant to Rule 66(B) and 68 of the Rules directing the Prosecution to (i) disclose any and all agreements between the Prosecution and witnesses who have testified or are scheduled to appear in this case; and/or confirm -- that's number (ii) that all such agreements in its possession or knowledge have been disclosed. On 7 July, 2014, the Prosecution responded that it communicated to the Defence that it had conducted a search for all relevant agreements relating to Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecution informed the Defence that with the exception of one agreement, which has already been disclosed, it had not located any such agreements. The Prosecution further stated in the responses that it is currently undertaking searches to determine whether it has any agreement concerning the witnesses identified on the Defence's Rule 65 ter witness list and will disclose any such agreements as and when they are located. Having considered the submissions of the parties, the Chamber is not satisfied that the Prosecution has failed to discharge its obligation under Rule 66(B) or Rule 68 of the Rules. The Chamber therefore dismisses the motion. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, before the break, we were just starting to look at P00329, and I think several of the computer screens were off and so I'll just start over with the introduction to this document. It's from the 12th of February, 1992. It's in Bapska. And it's the minutes of a meeting between the local civilian authorities and the assistant commander for civilian affairs. And it's -- indicates that the meeting was attended by five members of the Executive Council, as well as the local commune president and the secretary, also attended by the TO Defence commander and his deputy, a representative of the agricultural processing complex, and then representatives of the Bapska TO Staff, and then the president of the commission for resettlement and evacuation Branislav Jaric and a captain, a security officer from the Ilok counter-intelligence group. Do you know Branislav Jaric, the person here as the president of the commission for settlement and evacuation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the second page of the English, the bottom quarter of the page, it describes the progress of the meeting, and it's indicating here that before the beginning of the BD which is combat operations. I think the legend for that is somewhere. But BD, if I may suggest, refers to combat operations. Oh, it's right there. The village numbered 1750 inhabitants, 550 of whom remained after the liberation, Slovaks, 5 Hungarians, 518 Croats, of those remaining. And we'll talk more about numbers like this later. It's referring to 108 empty houses in the village. Is it true, Mr. Hadzic, that in Bapska and elsewhere throughout the SBWS during this period - early 1992 - it was local officials of Executive Councils and local communes who were involved in issues regarding settlement, particularly settlement involving houses that were left emptied by people who had left?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Bapska and the minutes, first, I have to say something we can all see, although I'm not understand -- everyone can understand. This was a meeting between organs of the military and organs of civilian authorities appointed by the military, so it is a meeting of the military administration because they all belonged to that part of the JNA. They had no consultations whatever with the SBWS government and no single appointment listed here had anything to do with the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Moving to page 3 of the English, the fourth full paragraph there, it says that at the meeting on 11 February, the local commune issued a decision to change the name of the village and that it should be called Arkanovo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it in the English version. Let me find it in the Serbian. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were aware that the local officials in Bapska wanted to change the name of Bapska to Arkanovo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware. How could I have been aware? If this situation were not so serious, this would strike me as ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, at least what they're purporting to do here is to change the name of Bapska and what they're doing is pursuant to the Law on Territorial Organisation that we discussed yesterday, which, under your legislation, actually empowered municipal councils to change the names of places such as this. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we discussed yesterday was one thing. This is military rule; it's a different thing. However, what you said about our discussion yesterday is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 508, P00138.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is the 5th of June, 1992, in Erdut. And what is happening here, Mr. Hadzic, is that the Erdut local commune and its president, Mr. Dokic, have issued a decision to transfer ownership of the building of the Serbian Volunteer Guard -- sorry. I will back up on. At its regular session on the 3rd of June, 1992, the executive committee discussed a request of the Serbian Volunteer Guard to approve to them, that is to say, to grant them, the use of the former Orasje local commune and made the following decision. The executive committee of the Erdut local commune hereby transfers ownership of the building to the Serbian Volunteer Guard. This is in Erdut, Mr. Hadzic. Do you know what is the property or the building that's referred to in this decision?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the building. I've never seen this document before. I only know that the Orasje local commune was on the right-hand side as one goes from Dalj to Most. I was not aware they had their premises though. That part of Erdut is called Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And indeed under the -- pursuant to the legislation we were talking about yesterday, the transfer of ownership of a facility like this to the Serbian Volunteer Guard would necessarily have to be consistent with the policy of your government otherwise this local commune would be acting beyond its authority. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this local commune did not work within its remit and in keeping with its authority, although I am not familiar with the document. I don't know anything about it. In my view, the municipality was the lowest level of socio-economic organisation that could do so. Local communes were on a different level and had to deal with some specific issues raised by inhabitants, but I cannot discuss this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually, from the earliest part of the conflict, isn't it local --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just last sentence of Mr. Hadzic was not translated. So he might repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the last part of my answer be back-translated to me so that I am reminded?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I could read it back, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, at page 38, line 7, your answer was: "I think this local commune did not work within its remit and in keeping with its authority, although I am not familiar with the document. I don't know anything about it. In my view, the municipality was the lowest level of socio-economic organisation that could do so. Local communes were on a different level and had to deal with some specific issues raised by inhabitants, but I cannot discuss this any further." And then that's apparently -- that's where it ends.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was some confusion. Local communes could only deal with some basic issues regarding the inhabitants, some local issues. I'm not certain they had the right to decide on property matters. I'm not certain, though, because I'm not a lawyer. I had been the president of the local commune in my village, and I know that we were not entitled to deal with such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 381, Exhibit P00168.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is the decision appointing a gentleman named Milan Ilic from Bijelo Brdo as president of the Executive Council of the Dalj municipality dated the 18th of December, 1991. This is an appointment that was approved or one that you signed off on in your capacity as prime minister?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Ilic prior to this date, the 18th of December? Did you know anything about his background or his profession?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Ilic was a high school teacher. I used to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1201, Exhibit P2415.2398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the Registrar has -- tells me that it is an under seal document, 1201.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then we would request to go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But your list doesn't indicate it as being confidential or under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. There's no problem, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we were talking about Ms. Negga, Blandine Negga, earlier. This is something that she wrote in June of 1992 directed to Mr. Thornberry. And we were talking about September 1992 before in Beli Manastir. And here we see she's writing about Beli Manastir - this is the third line of the document - referring to the incidents of murders, expulsion, threats, et cetera, particularly in the Baranja Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could see from the exhibits that most of the cases took place in Beli Manastir and that they were processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, skipping down three paragraphs, she refers to a meeting with local officials and writes: "Civil affairs and UNHCR accepted the invitation of the officials given at the meeting at Beli Manastir to attend a weekly meeting held each Monday at 9.00, together with the heads of councils of opstinas at Erdut. Only Mr. Milan Ilic was present. Since the abuses of human rights are proliferating and threats to both minorities and members of UNPROFOR are increasing, it was decided to lay these incidents before the council and ask their intervention in curbing the milicija and Red Berets and so compel the law enforcement branchs to do their duty." Mr. Hadzic, were you aware of Red Berets being present in the area of Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You became aware of it later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clearly remember that I was made aware of it in 1995 after an incident in which some people had been beaten up and then I was informed about it. Otherwise, I didn't know of their presence. I also heard that a residence which used to be a federal building had been plundered, and that the Red Berets were there before that, but that was also after 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here in the next paragraph she actually describes an incident involving torture of civilians by the Red Berets, acts of terror by the TDF - I'm not sure exactly what that is - against minorities: "The brutal murder of an old man by crushing his skull into the ground and the slitting of his throat within hearing distance of his 78-year-old mother, expulsion of property, people, and the immediate occupation of their houses and the beating of minorities," et cetera. Mr. Hadzic, you're the president of the RSK. This is June. Isn't it likely that you were hearing about incidents like this, such brutality and violence that was happening so frequently? You must have known. I'm going to put it to you one last time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see from this document that I was informed of it by Ms. Negga. Let me tell you this: Whatever I may have heard I never used my authority in order to obstruct any investigation or processing. I remember that in one of the indictments we could see here -- I seem to remember that a Hungarian had his skull crushed. I'm not sure if this was the same incident, but it was a matter for the court, and not me as the President. In any case, I'm trying to explain the following: Mr. Ilic, who we saw was appointed president of the Executive Council in Dalj, he was soon afterwards elected by the municipality for the Executive Council president in SBWS, so in a way became a regional government presided over by Milan Ilic. They were in charge of local policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have never seen in this trial one time that you ever spoke out against crimes being directed against non-Serbs. Did you ever actually go public and strongly criticise and condemn crimes like this? I don't think I've ever seen it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the fact that you didn't observe that, it's a different matter. But as of the day I turned 18 and became a rational person, I always treated everyone one the same, Serbs and Croats. It was completely normal for me to condemn any kind of injustice, as I do now. I don't see how you failed to observe that when I address the Court. I expressed my deepest regrets for the victims. If you want me to put it in even stronger words, I am very willing to do so. As for you not noticing, I'm not sure that's -- that is my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not noticing that you ver said anything about it in 1991 or 1992. And I'm not asking you about your personal views and what you tell us is your personal conduct. I'm asking you in your capacity as the leading Serb politician in Croatia at the time. You never once spoke out and condemned the criminals, Red Berets, the others who were doing these things in places like Beli Manastir and Erdut; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the question is unclear in the first sentence: "I'm not noticing that you said anything about it in 1991, 1992." I don't know what material or documents Mr. Stringer refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the fact that there are no materials or documents. I'm suggesting to the witness that we've never seen a document or a piece of evidence indicating that he publicly condemned crimes that we've been talking about today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, he refers to the material selected for this trial, by him. Or -- or something -- something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think the question is perfectly clear, Mr. Zivanovic. And Mr. Stringer can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me move on by asking you this, Mr. Hadzic. You've referred to the -- the judicial system and the proceedings in Beli Manastir. From that, can we conclude that essentially your way of dealing with crimes against non-Serbs is to simply passively let the judicial system run its course? That was -- that's your contribution?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for your use of the term "passive," I won't even comment on that. When I provided my previous answer, it was interpreted to me that I -- you said I never distanced myself from all these things. In any case, when discussing 1991 and 1992, any crimes that I was aware of I condemned, clearly. I said a few days ago, if you'll recall, speaking from the heart, that, at the time when the war was over, any crime committed against non-Serbs to me personally was as if a crime had been committed against me or a member of my family because it directly eroded the political position of the institution I tried to represent in the world. So I condemned it in the -- in the most serious way I could, and that included not only myself but all those who were my associates as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I would ask if the witness could repeat his answer. What was -- what he -- how -- how -- how it was translated to him the term that he was passive. Because I think that it is not transcribed or translated -- his answer was not accurately transcribed or translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this is about the term "passively," Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The part of his answer from line 16 to -- to line -- to line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Was all that not -- not correctly translated, Mr. Zivanovic? I -- I must say I'm a little bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was inaccurately translated or transcribed, I'm not sure. But I know what the witness said when he -- he answered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So this is about the question whether the witness ever condemned publicly in 1991 or 1992 these crimes. And you're asking for the witness to repeat his answer. So could the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Prosecutor said that I was passive, that is not correct. And when I said I didn't want to comment, that's because I didn't want to use a word that would not have been appropriate and therefore impolite. When I learned about a crime, I condemned it most severely. And I thought that the enforcement bodies had to work and do their job properly. Your Honours, if I am being labelled as passive, does it mean that I should have investigate crimes and arrest people as president of the republic? I thought that was not my job. If somebody thinks that I should have done that as well, then I am in the wrong. I really could not go around, roam the area and arrest people who had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask audiotape and correction of transcript or interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, coming back to this document we're looking at which is the Negga memo of 25 June, 1992, what she's writing about here is having described all of these things to Mr. Ilic in her meeting with him. And so then we see in the second full paragraph on page 2 of the English Mr. Ilic's response which is that while he was sympathetic, he himself had not committed any of the crimes and that indeed the same thing was happening on the other side. It was difficult to solve a century-old problem even 15 years. He held forth on the history of the area and the agreements reached in the early 1900s whereby the territory was decreed belonging to the Serbs and Croats and that they will divide the land and separate themselves one from the other. He eventually returned to the purpose of our meeting and pledged that at future meetings all local heads will be present and if we were unable to solve problems they could be specifically discussed at which point the local leaders would be called to account. Mr. Ilic was appointed by you to be in charge of the Dalj municipal council because he shared the policy of dividing the land and separating Serbs and Croats. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will comment upon this, although I really don't think that there is room for any comment. Milovan Ilic was appointed towards the end of 1991 at the proposal of the local communes of Dalj, Bijelo Brdo, and Erdut to become president of the Executive Council of the municipality of Dalj. A couple of months later, the regional assembly elected him as the president of the regional council in my absence and unbeknownst to me. When it comes to this meeting between Milan Ilic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you about what happened later. I'm asking about this meeting. So if you could just address the meeting which you're just about to do. We'll talk about Mr. Ilic's other positions in a minute.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, he was in a different position, not in the one that you mentioned. He attended that meeting as the president of the regional council. And if you will allow me, I would like to say that I have no include about that meeting. I'm not aware of his positions. I never heard what his positions were. I see this for the first time. This has absolutely nothing to do with me or anything else for that matter. At that time Milan Ilic on the 25th June was president of the regional council. He had been elected by the regional assembly, not by the government. At that time the government did not even exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The views expressed by Mr. Ilic here, I'm going to put to you, are the same views he held back in December 1991 when you appointed him to the Dalj municipal council. And all we're seeing here is that adherence to your policy. He's now risen to a higher level. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. I did not know anything about his positions either then or at the time when he attended his meeting -- this meeting. This is the first time I'm reading about those positions, if this indeed is correct. I did not appoint him as the president of the municipality of Dalj. I just signed off the government's decision that resulted from the proposal put forth by the local communes that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if his response to being confronted with all of these crimes and violence being directed against non-Serbs, if his response to all that is simply to point out that the other side is doing it too, that's also consistent with your own view and your own way of dealing with being confronted with crimes; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At any time, during 1991 through 1993.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. If Croatia was committing crimes -- crimes against Serbs and if somebody -- if the Republic of Serbian Krajina is committing crimes against Croats, they didn't have the right to do that. They should be – had to be arrested and tried. If Croatia didn't want to try its own criminals, I had nothing to do with that. When I pin-pointed problems, those were the problems of refugees, when Serbs were persecuted from Western Slavonia, arrived in Eastern Slavonia, and we did not know where to accommodate the Croats who would have wanted to return. We wanted reciprocity; i.e., we wanted Croats to go back to where they had come from in order for the Serbs to be able to come back to their own homes. This is the only time when I vote reciprocity. When it comes to committing crimes, there's no reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before the break, when I was asking you about Mr. Zivanovic in Beli Manastir, we were looking at those documents from September 1992 and there was a reference to a lot of Serbs coming in from Bosnia. Do you remember when we talked about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I recall correctly, your answer was that you didn't know anything about that at that time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that was not nebulous, that I didn't know anything about Serbs arriving from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 3 of the English. It's the fourth paragraph down from where we are currently in the B/C/S. There's a reference to a Mr. Kvesic, governmental representative for Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. Now I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Kvesic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Judging by the family name, he did not represent the Serbian community. He represented the Croatian community. Unless there's a mistake in the family name, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Here, he is referring to some 25 to 30.000 newcomers to that region from Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he is requesting clarification on UNPROFOR's position on that matter. The infiltration of Serbs who had not resided there prior to hostilities would certainly have a negative effect on initiating the process of return of displaced persons to the region as their houses would be occupied. How is it possible, Mr. Hadzic, that 25 to 30.000 newcomers could be coming into Baranja without your knowing anything about it, including people coming in from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll take this opportunity and give you an example to illustrate the whole situation. All who have arrived here have come via Amsterdam airport. Now, if somebody said that my family who had arrived from Serbia came from Amsterdam, because they passed through Amsterdam, that would be wrong. These are refugees from Croatia, from Western Slavonia, who had to travel by road via Bosnia, they passed through Bosnia by road. They are not from Bosnia. They are from Western Slavonia, but they passed through Bosnia, just like everybody arriving in Holland has to land in Amsterdam, including my family. I'm sorry for being so banal in my example. But I had to. I was aware of the refugees from Western Slavonia, but I never heard that these were refugees from Bosnia. I am aware of ten, 15, 100 people at the most who arrived from Bosnia. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that some 25.000 or so Serbs from outside Baranja were being resettled in the region, that they were coming to live in the region at this period of time, in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the exact number, but I know that a number of refugees arrived. They were not tourists. Their houses had been destroyed or burned down. They were expelled. They had to find accommodation somewhere. That's why they came. They didn't come of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, and they're coming there because there is empty, available housing that has been created for them by the expulsion of the Croats and the Hungarians and the other non-Serbs who were living there. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of Croats and Hungarians left the territory together with Croatian forces and those houses were preserved. Nobody destroyed them and their original owners, the same Croats, still live in those houses, and Hungarians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we've been looking today at reports like the one of Ms. Negga and the other documents about this campaign of terror and violence, what I'm saying is a campaign of terror and violence against non-Serbs in Baranja. Don't you see any connection between such a campaign directed against non-Serbs and the departure of non-Serbs from those areas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A majority of non-Serbs left the area together with Croatian authorities and the Croatian police, a vast majority. As for the crimes committed by individuals, those crimes were not organised by the authorities. Those were individual crimes committed by individuals which we tried to detect, elucidate, and process, and we managed in doing that. I condemned those crimes severely. I have always been against crime. I was against crime then and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 46, 65 ter 1D02759.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While it's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, this is something you've already referred to, just to get this confirmed. This is going to be a news report from the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It seems to be under seal, Mr. Stringer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologies. 2759.1, which will be the redacted one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do we have a tab number for that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We will -- we will check, Mr. President. The tab number I have is for the unredacted one, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a report. And here we see president Milan Ilic making a statement on behalf of this Vukovar regional council or I should say the regional council as an organ of the Grand People's Assembly of the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Could you just describe for us what was this body that he's now associated with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very clear. After the elections, after I was elected as the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, my position as the prime minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem remained empty. The same assembly that was convened for the first – for the second time on 25th of September, 1991, which elected the government in which I was the Prime Minister, was reconvened and elected the regional council for the region with a reduced number of minister and other things, but I didn't get involved in that. I was not part of that. Milan Ilic was elected as the president of the regional government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the region being SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So although it's a different title, is he sort of stepping into the shoes that you had held as the -- I don't want to say the prime minister but sort of the lead executive of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when I was in that position, the name of the body was the government and formally I was the president of the government. Later on, that was the Executive Council of the same body in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. The same assembly, consisting of 100 deputies, elected those people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, again, just to be clear on what Mr. Ilic's position, then, is, is he the -- is he the ranking executive, then, referring to executive or executive branch of the SBWS government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of that executive body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3220. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we now please have tab 582, Exhibit P3065.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, staying with Ilic and the regional council, this is the dated the 28th of October, 1992. It is a letter directed to a Mr. L. V. Moore, deputy chief of operations, Sector East. And we can look at the bottom, but it's a letter coming from Mr. Milan B. Ilic, president of the regional council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask the Registrar just to move to the bottom of the B/C/S version so that we can just confirm that. I apologise. The bottom of the original version, the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now going back to the top of the document, this relates to efforts of the international community to get access to the -- the site, the killing site at Ovcara, in order to conduct an exhumation. And Mr. Ilic here is indicating at the beginning that a letter that they had taken up at the regional council, Mr. Moore's letter concerning a request for permission for an exhumation of a possible mass grave in the area of the farm Ovcara near Vukovar. He says: "This question was considered at number 7 of the agenda and following conclusion has been achieved: That kind of permission we cannot sign or allow, not at this point of time, and not in the way you started possible actions on the mentioned questions."
