And then he continues on explaining his position on this. And, actually, in item 2, as I read it, Mr. Hadzic, he seems to be suggesting that it's possible that people buried at that location actually could have been parts of the Croatian armed forces, Ustasha, or I should say that it relates to a crime possibly committed by the Ustashas or the Croatian armed forces against civilian inhabitants would not been suitable for them and then now trying to shift the blame for that across to the Serb side. So do you remember this, Mr. Hadzic? You testified about the Ovcara exhumation and your involvement in getting it approved. Do you remember during this period of time Mr. Ilic actually was opposed in telling the international community that they would not allow access to the site?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I was not informed about that in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 658, P1909. And we would need to go into private session for this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 686, Exhibit P190.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. President. I believe this is also under seal. We'd need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we're going to shift gears a little bit here. I have been asking you about things said and done by others. Now I am going to ask you about some things said by you during these years, 1991 through 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 215, Exhibit P144.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as that's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, I can remind you about your testimony on the direct examination. You were asked to comment on this article during your direct. I'm looking at pages 9635 to 9639 of the transcript. And before we look at what you said on direct, let's just go to the part that you were asked to comment on in the article. In the -- under the third heading -- and just so we know, this is an interview with you as president of the SBWS government, 4th of September, 1991. And under the third heading there on the situation in SBWS now which territories are under the control of your government, this is what you say. And this is September 1991: "The best situation is in Baranja. Serbian liberators control 80 per cent of the territory ... Ustashas hold the border near Bilje. We expect entire Baranja to be liberated soon." And then we get to the part you were asked to comment on in your direct: "It's good for Baranja that the Hungarian population returned their arms given to them by Ustashas. They do not help us much in our fights, but they do not hinder us too as they recognise our sovereignty. The Croat, the native ones, the so-called Sokci, they are passive too. Croats, Herzegovina men, Dalmatians, even Zagorje men, all of them who settled after 1941, they are very dangerous as they know that one of our goals when we gain control is to return all Pavelic volunteers. That is incase they do not resist us. Incase they resist, then it is self-explanatory what will be with them." In your direct examination, Mr. Hadzic, you drew a distinction between more passive people who live in the flat land areas, if I can put it that way. You said that in your view are experienced people who come from mountainous regions tend to be more aggressive. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right from the start if we can talk about one group of people that you were looking to move out of SBWS, it would be descendants of Croats who came from Western Herzegovina during the Pavelic era. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke like that publicly but that was a political thesis of mine that in some way was not realistic. I wanted to cause some sort of political conflict between domestic Croats, peaceful ones and those who were aggressive. And in a way I drew to my side those Croats who were there from many years ago just like I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would this be the time for the break, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Stringer. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, at the time of the last break, we were looking at P144, and it is still on the screen. And I was asking you about your statement singling out or distinguishing between Croats in the region who were native, more passive ones, and then those who settled after 1941, the Herzegovinians and Dalmatians. And you had said that this was a political thesis of yours. You spoke like that publicly but it was a political thesis. In some way, not realistic. The reality is, Mr. Hadzic, isn't it, sir, that by singling out one group to be targeted, that is, Herzegovina Croats, you were signalling to all the people in the region that that particular group was one that could be lawfully singled out and targeted. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it's not. In keeping with my constitutional obligations according to the only state that existed at the time and that was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia I had a right and obligation to defend it. Like Mr. Vasiljevic said if he was a witness here that every sports club had the same obligation to defend the state. I defended my state from the people who attacked it and it was attacked most by the people from that region. They attacked the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, when you talk about returning all of Pavelic's volunteers, since we're talking about an era that was some 50 years prior to this, 1941 to 1991, in fact what you are talking about now are targeting people who are descendants of people who came after World War II. You're lumping them all together as a group that needs to be sent out. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. This is a political statement. Pavelic's volunteers were already very old at the time and the people who were born in the region enjoyed the same rights as I did. I wanted to cause a rift between the locals and the newcomers. But I did not have to do that because that rift had already existed. It pre-existed those events and it still exists in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, this was an irresponsible statement that you made, irresponsible as a leader of the Serbs, targeting any specific group of people based upon historical events of some 50 years ago. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I was not a career politician. I did not expect my political career to last more than a couple of months. I gave those statements without thinking much. I adapted them to the situation at hand. I really did not pay too much attention to any details, nor did I ever think what the implications of my statements could be, whether I could one day stand accused of crimes because of those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that the implications -- and you knew it at the time, the implications would be that at least as to one group of people living in that region, descendants of Herzegovina Croats, the implications are that they are now fair game to be targeted by the Serbian population throughout your district. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Those people that I had in mind were on the other side of the front line and their weapons were aimed at us. They could not be targeted either or more less based on my words. They targeted me. We targeted them in the same way. I could not make any decisions about them because they were on the other side, and from that side, they launched attacks on the state that we were trying to protect and preserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- before you move to the next paragraph, I would have a follow-up question for Mr. Hadzic. Mr. Hadzic, you say here that: "One of our goals is to return all Pavelic volunteers. That is in case they do not resist us. In case they resist, then it is self-explanatory what will be with them." That reads like a threat, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is what I said, it may sound like a threat, but I did not say that. This has been miscommunicated. How would they have been able to return under our authority given the fact that they were attacking us? It is completely illogical. This is a public session, so I would like to say that this was a big mistake on my part. I got to know these people later and they are the same as me. So I was totally mistaken when I called them what I did. But this is something that I hold against the locals. They like the people, they love their people just like I love mine. I am saying this more because of them than because of this trial and, of course, I have to say this for myself. I need to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What you were doing here, Mr. Hadzic, is exploiting the already existing ethnic tensions. Trying to divide the people, Croat against Croat, as well as Serb against Croat, and to exploit that in a way that would result in weakening the Croatian side or strengthening the Serbian side. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, of course it's not true. There were two sides in that war. I didn't have any intention. I was on one side and I wanted my side to prevail, for Yugoslav to be preserved, and for as many people as possible to join that cause and ultimately for the bloody war to be thwarted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The people who resisted the establishment of the Serbian Autonomous District of SBWS were going to be killed. Isn't that the threat that you're making here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Only those carrying arms and shooting at us could expect the same response from us. And those who were unarmed and who were not shooting at us, how should they have been killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we know now, don't we, after a year and a half of this trial, that hundreds and hundreds of unarmed people who were not shooting were in fact targeted, killed, and driven out of your Serbian Autonomous District only because they were not Serbs. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're putting it that way, but I can't confirm this. Your words were tendentious, you're saying "my Serbian district." At that time there was one and only state of Yugoslav and a lot of Serbs were expelled from Croatia which was one of its regions. I'm not justifying anything. I'm not justifying things that happened in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem for me expelling people from their homes is a crime. Hundreds of thousands of Serbs were expelled from Krajina. I'm not saying that -- because 250.000 people were expelled from Krajina, I'm not saying that they had the right to expel even one Croat from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. But it was war time. I could not influence any of these events. I didn't have a say. I couldn't say much at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just one last follow-up on that, Mr. Hadzic, and then we'll move on. But the fact is that you could in fact influence it and you did have a say, and that's what we're reading here in your public statements. You did have a say. And what you were saying was that, what we've just read here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that my words had any influence, you're welcome to your opinion. But from 1995 on, when we were left to our own devices, I mean, the Serbs in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, I did have a say but you know how that ended up. At that moment, I did not have a say. You know who drew all the strings. You know even better than I do who made all the decisions. I didn't have a say at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next paragraph here, you say: "The seat of our government is in Dalj. The part along the Danube river is free. Borovo Selo is in that area." So at this period in fact, the government was still located in Dalj, this being the 4th of September, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible. I don't remember. I said that at the beginning of September we were transferred to Erdut, but I can't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And because I noticed that if we go down a couple of the sections, if we move past "JNA Serbian fighters," if we move past "it is obvious co-operation" to the next heading that says "you have constituted the government," page 5 -- sorry, page 3 of the English. You say again there in paragraph 2, "The government is operating here in Dalj." So that, again, that would indicate to me that during this early September you were still based in Dalj as the government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not contrary to what I said. I don't know the exact date. In any case, at the beginning of September, we moved to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 32, 1D00826.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, this is backing up just a few days from the day of the earlier article. This is 29th of August. And this is in Beli Manastir, actually. An interview with you on the 28th of August, saying that Beli Manastir was visited by you on that day along with Ilija Kojic, Ilija Koncarevic. This is secretary-general of the government but perhaps that's a mistake. We know he was the president of the assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the text. Actually, the letters are too small. This is the journalist's interpretation. This just goes to show how correct journalists sometimes are in what they write.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's see if he's correct in some of the other things he is reporting here, these journalists. In the next paragraph, you're quoting as saying that: "The government has full control over the territory of SBWS. And we will endeavour to solve problems without much trouble." You continue to say: "About 80 per cent of the territory of Baranja has been liberated." And then you continue on to say -- first of all, let me ask just you to comment on that. When you say here, "80 per cent of Baranja had been liberated," that's probably about correct, isn't it, by the end of August? That was the case in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard that from somebody. I didn't tour the entire area to see it for myself. I can't read the text. The letters are too small and now everything is blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I can give you my copy of it, if you'd like to read from the hard copy. Again, it's small, but if you have the ability.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the letters are the same size, then there's no point. If the letters are a bit bigger, then, yes, please. Otherwise, no thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, mine are the same size, unfortunately. If we can do our best, what I'd like to read to you from the -- again the same paragraph in the English, and we'll see if we can get it set up for you better in the B/C/S. I see the Registrar has tried to make a larger copy.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly the same as your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's just see if we can work on the screen as best we can with it being enlarged there. The quote that's attributed to you that I'm interested in here is where you say: "We will invite all the Serbs outside Serbian countries, the Serbs from Zagreb, Rijeka, and other parts of the current Croatia who do not wish to stay in the Ustasha state, to come to Baranja, as Baranja is Serbian. There are [sic] empty houses here, which the Ustashas moved into after 1941, and they will not be coming back." Are you able to find that part of the text in the Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that part, but I can't read it. I don't remember that I said that. Not in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, would it then be a coincidence because, of course, just in the previous article from 4th of September, you're making a reference to, again, 1941 and those who settled after 1941, and so I'd suggest to you, sir, that it's no coincidence. You're in fact saying the same thing here, just on a different day.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't remember this. You can interpret my words any way you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But it would be consistent with what you've told us earlier, that this was a political strategy of yours to try to divide Croats between those who were the long-standing Croats who had been living in the region versus those descendents of Croats who came after 1941. So, again, if you're repeating that statement here, it is consistent with what was said earlier, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what you're doing here is to now sort of suggest the second -- the flip side, if you will, of the overall objective, which now that Croats are out, now that the houses are empty, you can encourage Serbs to arrive from other parts of Croatia in order to populate those empty houses and to contribute to changing the demographic ethnic composition of this area so that it will be Serb; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. The Serbs you mentioned, I don't see what towns they are from. They were already refugees. They had been expelled from Croatia and they were paying high rents for the emptied apartments in Bosnia and Serbia. They could come to Baranja and settle there temporarily until the moment their status was completely resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you say "temporarily," but, actually, it sounds a bit more permanent to me. According to the article here, you're quoted as saying, "The Ustashas who moved into --" should say, "Those who moved in after 1941," you say, "they will not be coming back." So this doesn't sound temporary, Mr. Hadzic, it sounds like a long-term programme in order to resettle Serbs into Baranja.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's not confront each other. There's a factual situation in Baranja. They returned. Their houses remained intact. The Serbs who were expelled from Western Slavonia, by contrast, their houses were destroyed, burned down, and they did not return. So we don't have to make any assumptions. The Trial Chamber is seized of facts and they know what happened just like God knows everything that happened. We're talking about past events. We are talking about something that is over. There's no need for any of us to make any assumptions because the facts are known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that this article, your quote here, doesn't refer to Western Slavonia. This refers to Serbs much farther away, in Zagreb and Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an even better example. That the Serbs from Zagreb and from all the other towns did not return to their places of origin, or, if they did, they did in very small numbers, or, as chemists would put it, in traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Moving down two paragraphs to the very bottom of page 1 of the English. This is the paragraph that begins with the words: "I am particularly pleased with the inter-ethnic relations on the ground ..." And then moving down to just two lines above the bottom of the page in English, we see a reference again to the -- the Sokci or the Catholic, as you say, the native Croats: "The Sokci, Catholic inhabitants of Backa, Srem, and Slavonia who are close to our mentality, never caused us any trouble. This evil has been brought upon the first, second and third peoples by the Croats, Herzegovinians, who, as Serbs, were converted 200 to 300 years ago." So, again, we're seeing, as we did in the previous article, Mr. Hadzic, you're referring to the -- the native Croats, as you referred to them. These are the more passive ones; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I don't recall that text, but that is how the journalist reported on it, and we can see that here. But I don't know what was said precisely. But when the journalist said that Ilija Koncarevic was the secretary-general of the government, if he made an error in such a basic important thing then we can imagine what sort of errors he could have made in things of minor importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You could be correct there, Mr. Hadzic, except, again, for that -- for the Chamber to accept your premise there, they'd have to conclude that it's just a complete coincidence that different couple of journalists are writing the same things down in another article, the one that we looked at previously, the one that your lawyer talked to you about during your direct examination; that's P144. Now we're with 1D826, and so, Mr. Hadzic, I'm putting it to you that this is not a coincidence. If fact, you did say these words. They're consistent with the words you've already said in the other article.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying now that we never had any problems with the native, peaceful Croats which shared -- who shared our views. And had I been asked and my Serbs from Slavonia and Baranja, the natives, as well as the Croats, native from there, there would never have been any war. The war would never have happened there at all. This is no secret. Even the Croats themselves say that. I used all my powers, everything that I had at my disposal, intellectual, and other powers I expended going to Zagreb attempting to prevent any possible conflicts that might have broken out. I could -- I didn't even assume that it would come to war. War happened independently of me. The Yugoslav army got involved. At that time I provided a statement for the newspapers but at that time nobody ever asked me about anything. Actually, nobody even read that among the population of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It wasn't even arriving there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down, there's a reference you've already alluded to, to Mr. Koncarevic. It says: "Speaking about the exchange of prisoners, Ilija Koncarevic said there were problems from the Croatian side, created by ... Seks by not respecting the agreement reached in Borovo Selo." And, again, just so we can all remember, Mr. Hadzic, Ilija Koncarevic, he was your minister of information, or was soon to be your minister of information, since this is not yet 25 September, 1991. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please read that name again and then remember yourself whether that is correct or not. Because it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're right. I'm wrong. Koncarevic was the -- he became on the 25th of September the president of the Great National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Here, we see him speaking about the exchange of prisoners, and he refers to Mr. Seks. Could you tell us who Mr. Seks was, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seks, at the time, was a representative of the Croatian authorities. I don't know what his function was at the time. Perhaps he was vice-president of the assembly or president of the assembly. But I remember that he was a commissioner for Slavonia and Baranja, appointed by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the problems or the issue of the prisoner exchange that Mr. Koncarevic is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it precisely. This is something that Koncarevic was in charge with, together with the federal government. Sometimes I would hear from him what was going on, but I didn't have any official information, and I didn't know any details. This was at the level of the JNA and the federal government. Koncarevic was included by the Serb side to make lists of Serbs that were on the Croatian side so that they could request an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: These prisoners were held in Beli Manastir? That's what's indicated here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: A few weeks after this -- and this is getting off the point just a bit, you recall the testimony of Ambassador Ahrens who talked about coming to meet with you in Borovo Selo in early September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That was evidently about ten days after this article. This was on the 6th or 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At that time, there were prisoners there at the police station in Borovo Selo; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that here from Mr. Ahrens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this into evidence, 1D826.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3221.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have tab -- could we have tab 229, Exhibit P2955.2913.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we have referred -- talked about this article already in the cross-examination. I think it was also something in your direct examination. It's an article from 20 September. And in paragraph 3 of the English there's a reference to Mr. Petrovic, the information minister, and that's the part I was asking you about before. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving down three paragraphs from there -- and I can give you my hard copy of this if you want to read it. It's a bit better than the last one.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. It's the article entitled, "the western borders of Slavonia are an open issue." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the title is: "The western borders of Slavonia are open."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On the bottom of the page of the English version, and for you, Mr. Hadzic, it's going to be the sixth paragraph, there's a quote attributed to you that says: "'People from Herzegovina, Imotska region, and Zagorje who were, however, colonised in our districts by Pavelic during the war will be given return tickets,' said Hadzic. Further to the question, 'Do you have problems with colonised Serbs who are extremists?' Hadzic replied, 'No, we do not.'" And then concludes, referring to your statement, that you belonged to a family that had lived in the district for the past 750 years. Here again, Mr. Hadzic, we see a journalist reporting in a publication during the very same period of time, a statement, again, where you refer to people colonised by Pavelic here, them being given return tickets. So, again, this is consistent with your political strategy of trying to distinguish between or divide so-called native Croats from Croats who came in the post-World War II era?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could conclude that from this, and that's what I said, that I used that as a sort of political game or platitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But the fact is a person reading this, particularly in the very insecure and ethnically charged environment in which these statements were being made at the time, someone reading this could indeed conclude that their soon-to-be prime minister is telling them it's okay to drive away people who were descendants of those Herzegovina Croats who arrived after 1941. Isn't it quite likely someone could conclude that it's okay to do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not very likely because I really didn't think that, and I didn't implement that. This was a statement calculated as a completely different effect, for a completely different effect, with the intention of bringing a certain section of Croats closer to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in the process, driving another section of Croats away, physically away. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would drive them away. They were already on the other side. They were the side that was shooting at our side. They were already on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that those people who had wives and children and grandparents, family members who were not shooting, and quite possibly Herzegovina Croats and other Croats who weren't participating at all in the conflict, they were all caught up in this as well, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. These people who stayed on our side, who did not shoot, they were the same for me as my mother and father and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is, Mr. Hadzic, when you or anyone else in a position of leadership sends a signal that it's okay to target a group that is different from yourself, that basically opens the door for targeting all groups that are unlike yourself. And isn't that what turned out in the end?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean, "in the end"? When the Serbs were expelled from the Krajina or at the end of the first part of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Hungarians who were expelled from Baranja, we'll talk about the numbers shortly, Hungarians who were expelled from the Planina area just above Erdut. It just doesn't stop with Herzegovina Croats; right? Once you've opened the door to it, everyone is at risk, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise. I didn't mean to provoke anyone. But you said "at the end," and that's why I asked which end did you mean. Because in my view, this did not happen at the end. It happened as part of the military clashes during the war. This is why I asked "at the end," when. I didn't mean to be provocative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're talking about this period August, September, right now. These are the dates of the articles we're talking about. And you say this was happening -- expulsions were happening during the period of the military conflict, but it's also true that the expulsions were happening at the same period when you were making public statements like this. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not receiving information at the time of any expulsions taking place. If you read carefully the text we read before these last two, I told you I was still waiting for a telephone line in Dalj. At the time we did not even have a phone line at our disposal to be able to work. So it was a nascent government with no conditions in place whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if innocent people who were descendants of Herzegovina Croats -- just them, if innocent descendants of Herzegovina Croats were expelled from the SAO SBWS during this period, would you accept responsibility for having contributed to that based upon these public statements you're making against them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone is expelling innocent people, no matter what their ethnic background, it's a serious crime in my eyes. It was not my intention to set such things in motion, such expulsions. It never even occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But now looking back on it as we sit here today, if that happened, would you accept responsibility for having contributed to it, based on having said this thing -- these things publicly at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago and apologise for having made that great mistake for dividing such people. They were just as good as me or the next person. But as I said, no one had even read this in Slavonia and Baranja. There was no impact. There was no electricity, they couldn't follow TV, and newspapers were not being sold. So there was no effect, at least not to the extent you expect it to have. In any case, I believe people should not be distinguished between no matter what they were born like. Croat, Serb, or Hungarian. The people I mentioned here were the people who, at the very beginning of the war, were on the other side, firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 428, Exhibit P37.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is the -- from the record of the notes -- sorry, the record of the meeting of the SFRY Presidency held on the 2nd of March, 1992. We're going to look at two parts of this. One part you looked at in your direct examination, and another part you did not. We can see from the first page here it's a list of all the people attending. You're there as president now of the RSK. You're accompanied by Mile Paspalj, who is president of the RSK Assembly; Mr. Zecevic, who was the prime minister; Veljko Dzakula was there; your RSK defence minister, Mr. Spanovic; and we can see all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we go to page 58 of the English and bottom of page 78 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Here we see, Mr. Hadzic, not your statement. We've been talking about things you've said. This is not something that you've said. This is something that was said by the prime minister who accompanied you to this meeting. And in the third paragraph of Mr. Zecevic's remarks, and he is referring to the situation in Benkovac. Now, we haven't spoken about Benkovac yet, but Benkovac is a town that's over in the Knin Krajina; right? It's not in the SBWS but it's, rather, in the Knin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I have the next page in the B/C/S version so as to follow what you were reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. It does continue over to 78. Sorry, 79. And what he says here is that: "It's not my intention to bother you with specific situation in Benkovac but the -- this town is specific when it comes to refugees. We're thinking only about our refugees. And we would like them to come back and they are welcome here. I'm in panic when I think that 15.000 Croats would return to Benkovac and they are mostly peasants emotionally linked to the soil. They are now compacted in Zadar area along the costal area. I fear the excess ignited by our people. This issue is a complex one. The instincts made our people burn anything that belonged to Croats in order to prevent them from coming back to their homes. The truth is that we cannot live together, that we do not want to live with them anymore. But there is also another type of truth, which is recognised by a democratic world, in which claims that these people have the right to return to their homes. I really cannot imagine how we are going to organise life then. I guess we will have to think about it later. I'm picturing it like this, well, gentlemen, the schools will teach Cyrillic and you hate it so much that you will simply have to leave. This is what is awaiting us." Now, Mr. Hadzic, we could go through this document, the rest of it. I'm going to suggest to you -- I'm going to put it to you that you sat passively by as the RSK prime minister said this. You didn't object or distance yourself from it because what he is doing here really is just setting out what was the RSK policy at the time and that was to prevent the Croat people from returning to Benkovac. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to answer your question the way you put it because you conclude that I sat there passively. I was not the person in charge of the meeting, and it was not my duty to correct each and every speaker. Now, if I thought the way you think, or if I thought the way an attorney thought -- would say that I didn't need deal with it. I don't want to be impolite but I didn't find it necessary to respond to the position of a person who said some words and who goes by a certain first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you share the views that were expressed by Mr. Zecevic here? Did you share the view at the time that --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do not share his views. Because of his political stance, Mr. Zecevic was replaced soon afterwards, perhaps not immediately but at some point later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's now talk about what you said when your turn came to speak. And this is also the same exhibit, P37. And now we're going to move to page 68 of the English, page 92 of the B/C/S. And, Mr. Hadzic, this is the part that you were asked to comment on in your direct examination, and I've got some follow-up questions about it. And we can actually move back a few pages, if you'd like. Perhaps you'll accept my suggestion that who's talking here above you, who is speaking before you begin to speak, is Radovan Karadzic, who was also attending this meeting, and this is the passage where there's the discussion about whether it was nebulous to think about Serbs moving in from elsewhere. Do you remember this issue?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this comment of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again, Dr. Karadzic is observing or saying: "But who is going to make the Croats from Vojvodina to move to Krajina? These are nebulous ideas seen as abhorrent by the rest of the world, though India and Pakistan did exactly the same thing." He goes on to say: "It is rather questionable if anything like that would be feasible in Europe at the moment. I mentioned this only to make you cognizant of their way of thinking and of their hopes. Their greatest hopes are invested in your gradual migration as you will not be organised enough and thus enable to hold on down there." And this is where you say: "There is nothing nebulous in it. The Serbs from Zagreb should resettle, as well as those from Belgrade, and it is out of the question now." Mr. Hadzic, we've been talking a lot of about Croats and other non-Serbs going out. It was also part of the plan and the policy, actually, to resettle Serbs into the RSK from other parts, not because they necessarily have been driven away, but, actually, just to, again, solidify and to consolidate Serb demographic control over all areas of the RSK. Wasn't that your policy? Resettlement: Serbs in; Croats out.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my policy. Perhaps it was interpreted slightly differently as if you said that the Serbs left Croatia voluntarily, that they had not been expelled. I simply wanted to ask you if it is your position in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Our position is that it was RSK policy to resettle Serbs into -- sorry, to resettle Serbs into areas controlled by the RSK and by the SBWS. Among those Serbs being resettled were unquestionably Serbs driven out of other areas of Croatia such as Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. It is clear now. As regard this is sentence, I was interrupted and did not continue. Then Sejdo Bajramovic took the floor. I said that it was nebulous because it already happened, the Serbs had already been expelled from Zagreb and they were supposed to resettle in Belgrade, according to the Croatian plan at least, and that the Serbs from this area could not be driven out. There was no mention of that. A Serb from our territory would not resettle in Belgrade. That's what I was trying to explain. This discussion was not only about Serbs but Croats as well. I said that this had already happened to the Serbs. That this process had been completed by then. That the Serbs had left the large cities of Croatia and that was not something that we had to decide about. It was already 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to put it to you, Mr. Hadzic, that in fact what you're saying here, what you're defending as something that is not nebulous, is in fact a policy that goes back to the very earliest part of 1991 when you were associated even with the SNC, when it was about firstly delineating borders, and, secondly, moving populations in order to separate Serbs from Croats. And if we fast forward now to this meeting in March of, 1992, about 14 -- 13, 14 months later, it's the same policy. And that's what you're referring to here, isn't it? Continuation of establishing a border and then moving populations, exchanging them, in order to separate the people.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are completely off. I simply responded to Karadzic's words. I said that it was not a point of discussion because the Serbs had already been expelled from large towns and went to Belgrade. They did not come to Krajina. They did not come to the area. So it has nothing to do with what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 705, P2327.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, before I ask you about -- well, if we could just scroll to the next page of the B/C/S, please. This is an interview with you as president of the RSK entitled, "Osijek shall be Serbian." And before I ask you about what's contained in it and we could enlarge it, if necessary. The bottom right-hand corner of what you're looking at, Mr. Hadzic, can you see the date? Can you tell us what the date of this publication is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now perhaps if we can zoom out a bit just so that you can see more of the article generally. Do you recall this interview? Do you recall having spoken to this person in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. And I can't see the name of the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a couple of parts of this and then -- and in fact my version of this is bigger, if you'd like to have it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What I'd like to take you to, Mr. Hadzic, is on page 2 of the English. You were asked a question. The question is: "You think that there shall be no more saboteurs? Then you answer. Your answer begins: "No, there shall only be some exchanges of fire along the border." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me at least approximately where it is in Serbian? I was reading the text so I wasn't listening carefully. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the fourth question you were asked: "You think there shall be no more saboteurs?"

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your answer there you say: "There shall only be some exchanges of fire along [sic] the border." And then continuing: "All we need to do is to correct the border to Eastern Slavonia so that Osijek and Vinkovci can become a part of the Serbian state." And, again, you were asked under what conditions. And your answer: "It would be done in such a manner that Serbs from Rijeka, Pula, Zagreb, and other Croatian cities would move to Osijek and Vinkovci. "Q. What would Croatia receive in return for Osijek and Vinkovci?" And you say: "Apartments, houses, farms, vast wealth owned by urban Serbs who left Croatia already. 2- or 300.000 people." And your next answer you say: "Yes, I'm talking about a peacetime solution, the reasonable solution. At the moment it is 99 per cent unachievable. This is why I think that we shall get Osijek and Vinkovci in an escalation of conflict initiated by the Croatian side." So, despite what you've said repeatedly about these resettlements being of a temporary nature, what we're seeing here is actually what you had in mind as a long-term permanent solution to what you saw as the problem, and your solution was to simply resettle Serbs from other areas of Croatia and to separate Croatian and Serb people from each other. That's your solution to the problem, as you see it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I will not ask you whether it is really your opinion because I don't want to appear provocative, but at that time, in 1993, in Rijeka and Zagreb there were no Serbs left. And even if there were any Serbs, it didn't even occur to them to move there. I don't remember this interview, nor this journalist. I have never heard of him, and I don't think I have ever given this interview. If I did, it must have been part of a pre-election campaign or trying to divert or deter a Croatian attack that I was convinced was forthcoming. I just wanted to make a sort of hollow threat, trying to protect the people of Slavonia and Baranja – the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was not only unreal, it was crazy. Osijek alone as the city had a larger population than the entire Serbian District. As for all Serbs coming from Zagreb and Rijeka, it would not have been even up to 10 per cent of the Osijek population. It simply wasn't an option that was discussed. I'm not sure I gave this interview. If I did, I was trying to deter Croatia from attacking us, threatening that we could then take Osijek, but we neither wanted that, nor would we have been able to do it. And even when the JNA could have taken Osijek in 1991, of course it did not take it, why would it take Osijek – well, and at the time I could not exert any influence on the JNA in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the last exhibit on this, Mr. President. It would be really a great breaking point if I could just get through the last exhibit because it then moves into a whole new subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would need a few -- a few minutes -- for a few administrative matters, Mr. Stringer, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Maybe I'm pushing my luck because it's a videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If it's really wrapping up an important issue, I think we better go on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This would be tab 1000, P2886. And what we can do here is start -- I'm interested in the text that begins at page 4 of the transcript which is at time code 3 minutes, 27.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have page 4. We will simply have to find the right part on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're just about there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: A moment ago, you mentioned Republika Srpska. How do we co-operate with them? "Goran Hadzic: Serbian people in these territories must live together. Practically speaking, they must live in one state; formally speaking, it is of the least importance how this state is going to be called. After the referendum here and in Republika Srpska, it is clear that we will live unified and together. We have to agree everything with Republika Srpska, practical issues related to the unity, and after that the formal issues as well. In addition to the practical issues that are already being dealt with by unified parties, we expect that the Serbian Democratic Party of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and of Republika Srpska will soon be unified. "Journalist: Today you attended a meeting of the Regional Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. What are your impressions? "Goran Hadzic: I am satisfied with the work of the party in this area, where we are now, especially in Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem. I am not satisfied about other parts of Krajina where some individual mistakes have been done, like setting up of fractions. However, we are on our way to unify all the fractions and to build up again a strong party of the Serbian people. I can tell you that with full responsibility that I am sure we will realise that because none of all the leaders of all individuals who have, in a way, chosen to follow another direction, did not turn away politically from the final goal, the self-determination. This the final goal, that the Croatian and Serbian people don't live together. So all our other disputes should be considered as our internal matters and people should not worry about that. However, the people are worried, but there is no reason for that. I mean, we are unified with regards to the final goal of our Serbian journey. "Journalist: Mr. President, you are the president of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Do you have something you would like to tell your people? "Goran Hadzic: Well, I can tell you that we have come quite some distance on this journey and it is evident that the objective has been accomplished. The Serbian people will live in one state and that's what we want for other nations as well, to live together. And we will strive to that goal that the Croatian people will live together as well as the Slovenian. Muslims will receive their small state and everybody will be happy. "Journalist: But in the case of aggression against our territory, what will happen to them? "Goran Hadzic: In the case of aggression against our territory, it is clear that Croatia cannot fight even against the Republic of Serbian Krajina, so in case they would choose to fight us and Republika Srpska, I think the Croats in Zagreb should think carefully about the place where to evacuate."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just really briefly, Mr. Hadzic. What you said here was actually your view, and it was the policy of the RSK, and that's that the final goal that the Serbian and Croatian people don't live together. This is in 1993. It was the goal from the beginning, and it was the goal in 1993 as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the goal from the beginning and in 1993, and I said that in the election campaign. We wanted to stay in Yugoslavia. That was our goal, but I knew already then that Yugoslavia had formed a separate constitution. I could not say that publicly, and the way I did so I was saying what I had to say. But it was already clear in which direction we were moving. And that was not the direction that I was talking about just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That would be my last question for today, Your Honour, but not for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Before we adjourn, I would like the parties to give us an indication, if they can, for planning purposes of the remaining time Mr. Hadzic will be on the witness-stand after the recess. Mr. Stringer, you are now at 17 hours cross. Do you have any indication to give us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, in theory, I think that would leave us with about 14 or 15 hours, which my sincere hope would be not to have to use all of that. But to be honest, Your Honour, I have -- I cannot say for sure when we're back in court on the 18th of August, whether what I've prepared at that time will -- will go for 15 hours or whether it would go for 12. I think that it's fair to assume that with the redirect examination, assuming there would be re-direct, that we could count on filling that first week back. But I would certainly strive to time it so that we do not extend into the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you have any indication about eventual re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will have re-direct. That is certain. But I cannot say my estimate at this point of time before the Prosecution complete his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Hadzic, the Court will adjourn for three weeks now. For the duration of the recess, you remain a witness and under oath. You therefore cannot discuss your testimony with anyone, except as provided for in our access to counsel decision of 2 July, 2014. So the parameters of our access to counsel decision remain in effect. I wish everyone in and around the courtroom either a happy vacation period or a productive non-sitting time, or, if it so happens, both. One last thing for which I'm asking everyone's attention. After the recess, the Court will resume not on Monday but on Tuesday, 19 August. But the Court will, nevertheless, sit four days that week, which means from Tuesday till Friday, Friday included. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of August, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 25
